topic.name: Approximating Areas With the Trapezoidal Rule

question.text: The rate, in degrees Farhenheit per month, at which the average midday temperature in New York City varies, does so according to the function $R(t) = t^3+3,$ where $t$ is the number of months since the measurements began. Estimate the total increase in air temperature over the first three months using the trapezoidal rule with $3$ trapezoids of equal height.
question.explanation:
In this context, the area $\mathcal{A}$ under the curve $y = R(t)$ over the interval $[0,3]$ represents the total increase in air temperature over the first three months.

The general formula for the trapezoidal rule states that \[ \mathcal{A} \approx \frac{1}{2}\left[R(a)+ 2(R(t_1) + R(t_2) + \cdots + R(t_{n-1})) + R(b) \right]\Delta t, \] where $n$ is the number of trapezoids and $\Delta t = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ is the step size.

Here, we have the following values:

  • The number of trapezoids is $n=3.$

  • The corresponding interval is $[0,3],$ so we have $a=0$ and $b=3.$

  • The step size is given by \[ \Delta t = \dfrac{b-a}{n} = \dfrac{3-0}{3} = 1. \]

Using the above values, the general formula becomes \[ \mathcal{A} \approx \dfrac{1}{2}\left[R(0)+ 2\left(R(1) + R(2) \right) + R(3) \right]\cdot 1. \]

To identify the function values, we now set up a table with the values of $t$ and $R(t)\mathbin{:}$

$t$ $0$ $1$ $2$ $3$
$R(t)$ $3$ $4$ $11$ $30$

Substituting the appropriate numbers into the above expression gives

\begin{align*} \mathcal A &\approx \dfrac{1}{2}\left[3+ 2(4 + 11) + 30 \right] \cdot 1 \\[5pt] % &= \dfrac{1}{2}(63) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{63}{2}\\[5pt] & = 31.5. \end{align*}

Therefore, the total air temperature increase is approximately $31.5^\circ \, \textrm{F}.$

example.title: Using the Trapezoidal Rule: Word Problem

question.text:
Using the trapezoidal rule with the partition \[ [-1,2] = [-1,0] \cup [0,2], \] approximate the area under the curve of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ whose data is given in the table below.

$x$ $-1$ $0$ $2$
$f(x)$ $1$ $3$ $2$
question.explanation:
Let's plot what this function might look like, using the values given in the table.

We've drawn some trapezoids to help calculate our trapezoidal rule sum. By calculating the area of each trapezoid, we obtain the following approximation for our area $\mathcal{A}\mathbin{:}$ \[ \mathcal{A} \approx \overbrace{ \left[\: \dfrac{\overbrace{ \color{red} f(-1) {\color{black}+} f(0) } ^{\large\color{red}\textrm{bases}}}{2} \!\cdot\! \underbrace{ \color{blue} \Delta x_1 }_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{height}} \:\right] }^{\Large\textrm{$1$st trapezoid}} + \overbrace{ \left[\: \dfrac{\overbrace{ \color{red} f(0) {\color{black}+} f(2) } ^{\large\color{red}\textrm{bases}}}{2} \!\cdot\! \underbrace{ \color{blue} \Delta x_2 }_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{height}} \:\right] }^{\Large\textrm{$2$nd trapezoid}} \]

Substituting the appropriate numbers into the above expression gives \begin{align*} \mathcal{A} &\approx \dfrac{{\color{red}1}+{\color{red}3}}{2}\cdot ({\color{blue}0 - (-1)}) +\dfrac{{\color{red}3}+{\color{red}2}}{2}\cdot ({\color{blue}2 - 0})\\[5pt] &= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}1} +{\color{red}\dfrac{5}{2}} \cdot {\color{blue}2}\\[5pt] &= 2 + 5 \\[5pt] &= 7. \end{align*}

example.title: Using the Trapezoidal Rule With Irregular Step Size

question.text:
Using the trapezoidal rule with the partition \[ [0,5] = [0,2] \cup [2,5], \] approximate the area under the curve of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ whose data is given in the table below.

$x$ $0$ $2$ $5$
$f(x)$ $3$ $1$ $4$
question.explanation:
Let's plot what this function might look like, using the values given in the table.

We've drawn some trapezoids to help calculate our trapezoidal rule sum. By calculating the area of each trapezoid, we obtain the following approximation for our area $\mathcal{A}\mathbin{:}$ \[ \mathcal{A} \approx \overbrace{ \left[\: \dfrac{\overbrace{ \color{red} f(0) {\color{black}+} f(2) } ^{\large\color{red}\textrm{bases}}}{2} \!\cdot\! \underbrace{ \color{blue} \Delta x_1 }_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{height}} \:\right] }^{\Large\textrm{$1$st trapezoid}} + \overbrace{ \left[\: \dfrac{\overbrace{ \color{red} f(2) {\color{black}+} f(5) } ^{\large\color{red}\textrm{bases}}}{2} \!\cdot\! \underbrace{ \color{blue} \Delta x_2 }_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{height}} \:\right] }^{\Large\textrm{$2$nd trapezoid}} \]

Substituting the appropriate numbers into the above expression gives \begin{align*} \mathcal{A} &\approx \dfrac{{\color{red}3}+{\color{red}1}}{2}\cdot ({\color{blue}2 - 0}) +\dfrac{{\color{red}1}+{\color{red}4}}{2}\cdot ({\color{blue}5 - 2})\\[5pt] &= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}2} +{\color{red}\dfrac{5}{2}} \cdot {\color{blue}3}\\[5pt] &= 4 + \dfrac{15}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{23}{2}. \end{align*}

example.title: Identifying Whether the Trapezoidal Rule Sum Gives an Underestimate or Overestimate

question.text: An empty tank starts filling with water according to the function $v(t)=t^2-3t+7,$ in liters per minute. Use the trapezoidal rule with the partition \[ [0,2] \cup [2,5] \cup[5,7], \] to approximate the total amount of water in the tank the first $7$ minutes.
question.explanation:
In this context, we have $3$ trapezoids, and the area $\mathcal{A}$ under the curve $y = v(t)$ represents the total amount of water in the tank the first $7$ minutes.

Using the trapezoidal rule, we estimate the area as follows: \[ \mathcal{A} \approx \dfrac{v(0) + v(2)}{2} \cdot \Delta t_1 + \dfrac{v(2) + v(5)}{2} \cdot \Delta t_2 + \dfrac{v(5) + v(7)}{2} \cdot \Delta t_3 \]

To identify the function values, we now set up a table with the values of $t$ and $v(t)\mathbin{:}$

$t$ $0$ $2$ $5$ $7$
$v(t)$ $7$ $5$ $17$ $35$

Substituting the appropriate numbers into the approximation for $\mathcal{A}$ gives \begin{align} \mathcal{A} &\approx \dfrac{7 + 5}{2} \cdot (2 - 0) + \dfrac{5 + 17}{2}\cdot (5 - 2) + \dfrac{17 + 35}{2}\cdot (7 - 5) \\[5pt] & = 6(2) + 11(3) + 26(2)\\[5pt] &= 12 + 33 + 52 \\[5pt] &= 97. \end{align}

Therefore, the total amount of water in the tank is approximately $97 \, \textrm{liters}$ the first $7$ minutes.
